title: E38-Based BMW M7 Prototype Had M5 Power and a Six-Speed Manual

body_markdown:
BMW has sold M-branded variants of the 7 Series in the past, but it has never marketed a full-blown M7 to take on AMG’s version of the Mercedes-Benz S-Class. The brand could have pioneered this segment 30 years ago, however. The one-of-a-kind, E38-based BMW M7 featured a naturally aspirated V-8 borrowed from the E39-generation M5, a six-speed stick, and a 155-mph top speed.


Revealed by BMW Classic, the design study was based on a short-wheelbase 1997 740i. BMW pulled out the stock 4.4-liter V-8 and replaced it with the 4.9-liter V-8 (called S62 internally) that it was designing for the then-upcoming[E39-gen M5](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/bmw-e39s-are-the-best-buy-in-v-8-stick-shift-sedans/) . The eight-cylinder developed 400 horsepower at 6600 rpm, and it sent that power to the rear wheels via a six-speed manual transmission.


BMW


BMW


For context, the 740i’s stock V-8 was rated at 282 horsepower, and BMW never sold the E38 with a stick in the United States. Had it reached showrooms shortly after the prototype was built, the M7 would have competed in a class of one. AMG made a handful of[W140](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/for-all-its-foibles-was-the-w140-s-class-the-last-proper-mercedes-benz/) -based S-Class models, but buyers who wanted a mass-produced, AMG-tuned S-Class had to wait until the S55 made its debut for 2001. Based on[the W220-generation model](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/mercedes-benz-s-class-a-history-of-firsts/) , it was powered by a naturally aspirated, 5.4-liter V-8 engine rated at 355 horsepower.


> [View this post on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DfxYwRrOHxj/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)
>
>
> [A post shared by BMW Classic (@bmwclassic)](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DfxYwRrOHxj/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)


BMW Classic didn’t release performance figures, but it noted that the M7 prototype weighed about 4130 pounds. That’s slightly less than the American-market 740i, which weighed 4255 pounds, and the S55 AMG, which tipped the scale at 4190 pounds. And while the 400-horsepower output doesn’t sound like much in 2026, it was a lot for the era: Ferrari’s 355 made 380 horsepower.


Visually, the M7 prototype looked pretty much like the 740i with the exception of BBS wheels and quad exhaust outlets. It offered all of the features 7 Series buyers expected in the 1990s, including power-adjustable rear seats and a phone in the center console.

BMW


There’s no word on why the BMW M7 wasn’t approved for production. Nothing suggests that[the current-generation 7 Series](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/2023-bmw-760i-xdrive-and-i7-xdrive60-review-dual-dreamboats/) will spawn the first M7, either; We don’t think BMW dusted off the concept to preview an upcoming model. Instead, the company’s post serves a cool, behind-the-scenes look into the 7’s history—and a confirmation that the E39 M5’s drivetrain fits in an E38, in case any of you would like ideas for your next project..
